articles.summary: Kansas City needs someone who can threaten defenses, command attention and give Mahomes another experienced target
articles.body:
T he Kansas City Chiefs are 4-0, one of only three undefeated teams remaining in the NFL and suddenly looking like a legitimate Super Bowl contender again. But Sunday's dramatic 30-27 victory over the Las Vegas Raiders came with a potentially significant cost.

Kansas City lost both Rashee Rice and Tyquan Thornton to injuries, leaving a wide receiver room that was already facing questions suddenly in need of reinforcements. For a team coming off a disappointing 2025 season, the timing could hardly be more important. The Chiefs have put themselves in position to make another run at the Super Bowl, but they can't afford to let injuries at receiver undermine an offense that is beginning to find its rhythm.

The obvious solution is the free-agent market. Kansas City doesn't necessarily need to find another superstar. It needs someone who can step into the rotation, understand the offense and give Patrick Mahomes another reliable option while Rice and Thornton recover. Here are four veteran receivers the Chiefs could consider.

If Kansas City wants the biggest possible name, the answer is obvious. Tyreek Hill remains available more than a year after suffering a serious knee injury, and the Chiefs reportedly are among the teams that could be interested in bringing him back to where his NFL career became a phenomenon.

A reunion would make sense on multiple levels. Hill spent his first six seasons with Kansas City, becoming one of the league's most dangerous deep threats while developing a devastating connection with Mahomes. His speed changed how defenses had to play the Chiefs, and putting him back in the same offense would give Kansas City an intriguing short-term solution.

The question is whether Hill can still be that player. Tyreek, 32, acknowledged in July that he still had "no power" in his injured leg. That raises obvious questions about his explosiveness and how quickly he could return to an NFL workload.

Kansas City also would have to determine how much Hill has left physically and whether he could contribute immediately. But the Chiefs don't need the 2018 version of Hill . They need someone who can threaten defenses, command attention and give Mahomes another experienced target. If Hill is healthy enough to play, Kansas City may be the most natural destination.

DeAndre Hopkins offers something very different from Hill. Hopkins isn't a burner at this stage of his career. He's a veteran possession receiver whose value comes from his experience, route running and ability to win contested catches.

Hopkins spent the 2025 season with the Baltimore Ravens in more of a complementary role and subsequently joined Georgia Tech's offensive coaching staff. He has made clear, however, that he hasn't retired. That distinction could become important if Kansas City comes calling.

Hopkins already knows what it takes to play at the highest level, having spent his career dealing with double teams, changing quarterbacks and defensive schemes designed specifically to limit him.

For the Chiefs, he wouldn't need to become their No. 1 receiver. He could simply become a veteran target who understands how to find space and make difficult catches when Mahomes needs someone he trusts. At this stage of his career, that could be enough.

Gabe Davis is the more intriguing reclamation project. Davis hasn't been able to reproduce the production that made him an important piece of Buffalo's offense early in his career. His stint with Jacksonville didn't go as planned, and he returned to Buffalo for part of the 2025 season.

Then came another setback. Davis suffered an ACL injury in January, leaving his availability and conditioning as major questions. He's now roughly nine months removed from the injury, though, meaning a return could become increasingly realistic as the season progresses.

The Chiefs would have to determine how close Davis is to his pre-injury form. If healthy, however, his skill set would make sense in Kansas City. Davis has experience as a downfield threat and has shown an ability to make plays in an offense where defenses can't devote all their attention to him.

He would represent more of a calculated gamble than an immediate solution, bu t the Chiefs have the luxury of being 4-0. They can afford to think beyond this week.

Noah Brown might be the least glamorous name on the list, but he could be one of the most practical. The Raiders released Brown at the end of training camp, and he remains available after failing to find another NFL roster.

Brown has never been a consistent star, but he has produced more than 500 receiving yards in seasons with both the Dallas Cowboys and Houston Texans . He also became part of NFL highlight-reel history with his memorable Hail Mary catch while playing for Washington.

That résumé could be enough for Kansas City to take a look. Brown wouldn't be expected to replace Rice or Thornton. Instead, he'd provide another experienced body capable of playing snaps while the Chiefs sort out their injury situation. And unlike a player coming off a major injury, Brown could potentially offer Kansas City a quicker path to contributing.

For a team that just lost two receivers in the same game, that matters. Kansas City doesn't need to panic, yet. The Chiefs ' 4-0 record changes the equation. They're not trying to save a season. They're trying to protect one that has already put them in an excellent position. That's why Kansas City doesn't necessarily have to chase the biggest name available.
